procedural_history.originating_court: Special Magistrate of Nagpur, Madhya Pradesh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Prosecution proceedings before the Special Magistrate
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The questions raised in the Supreme Court petition appear to have been raised before the High Court at previous stages by means of applications under Article 226 and decided against. No appeals to the Supreme Court were taken against those orders.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Petitioners approached the Supreme Court directly under Article 32 of the Constitution to quash the proceedings before the Special Magistrate, arguing that their fundamental rights were violated. The Supreme Court discouraged the practice of direct approach to the Supreme Court in matters that have been taken to the High Court and found against, without obtaining leave to appeal therefrom.

issue.issue_text: Whether the allotment of an individual case to a Special Magistrate under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure Code, who has to try the case under the normal procedure, results in discrimination under Article 14 of the Constitution.

facts: An individual case was allotted to a Special Magistrate appointed under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The Special Magistrate was required to try the case entirely under the normal procedure.
law: Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees the right to equality and prohibits discrimination.

The precedent in *Anwar Ali Sarkar's case* established that discrimination under Article 14 occurs when an individual case is sent to a special court that uses a procedure substantially different from the normal one, thereby prejudicing the accused compared to others who committed similar offenses.
application: The Court distinguished the current case from the precedent set in *Anwar Ali Sarkar's case*.
It reasoned that the principle from *Anwar Ali Sarkar's case* only applies when the special court uses a procedure that is materially different from the normal one.
In this case, the Special Magistrate had to follow the normal procedure entirely.
Therefore, there was no different or prejudicial procedure being applied, and no discrimination of the kind contemplated in the precedent case arose.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the allotment of a case to a Special Magistrate is not discriminatory under Article 14 of the Constitution as long as that magistrate has to try the case under the normal procedure. A law that vests such discretion in an authority is not unconstitutional.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sanction for prosecution is invalid because the sanctioning order does not disclose that all the facts constituting the offences were placed before the sanctioning authority.

facts: The petitioner challenged the validity of the sanction for prosecution, arguing that the sanction order did not show that all the facts of the case were placed before the sanctioning authority.
This argument was based on the Privy Council case of Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King.
The trial in the current case had not yet commenced.
The counsel for the State informed the court that evidence would be presented during the trial to prove that all necessary facts were indeed before the sanctioning authority.
law: The Supreme Court referenced the same Privy Council case (Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King) relied upon by the petitioner.

The Court noted that the Privy Council itself had recognized that any 'lacuna' (defect or omission) in a sanction order, such as the failure to list all facts, can be remedied during the course of the trial by presenting specific evidence to that effect.
application: The Court applied the principle that a defect in a sanction order is curable.
Since the trial had not yet started, there was an opportunity to present evidence to remedy the alleged defect in the sanction.
The State's assurance that it would provide such evidence at trial further supported the decision to not invalidate the sanction at this preliminary stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, concluding that it was unnecessary to decide whether the sanction was invalid as it stood. The Court reasoned that any potential defect in the sanction order could be cured with evidence presented during the upcoming trial, as established by the very precedent the petitioner cited.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power of the sanctioning Government to specify a court for trial under section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code excludes the power of another authority to appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14 of the Code.

facts: A public servant of the Madras Government was being prosecuted in Madhya Pradesh.
The Madras Government sanctioned the prosecution under section 197(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The Madras Government did not, however, exercise its power under section 197(2) to specify the court where the trial would be held.
The Madhya Pradesh Government appointed a Special Magistrate to try the case under section 14 of the Code.
law: Section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code gives the government that sanctions a prosecution the discretionary power to specify the court for the trial.
Section 14 of the Criminal Procedure Code allows a Provincial Government to appoint a Special Magistrate for the trial of particular cases.
application: The petitioner argued that only the sanctioning government (Madras) could specify a special court under section 197(2), and its failure to do so meant that another government (Madhya Pradesh) could not appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14.
The Supreme Court rejected this argument, calling it a "misconception of the respective scopes of the powers" under the two sections.
The Court drew a key distinction: section 197(2) relates to specifying a "Court," whereas section 14 relates to appointing a "person" (a Special Magistrate).

It held that the power under section 197(2) is "permissive" and "optional." If the sanctioning government chooses not to specify a court, the trial is simply governed by the other provisions of the Code, which includes the power to appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14.

The Court also dismissed the idea that section 197(2) was for the protection of the public servant. It stated this power is for administrative reasons, such as convenience or the complexity of the case.
Therefore, the exercise of power by the Madhya Pradesh Government under section 14 was not excluded or nullified by the non-exercise of power by the Madras Government under section 197(2).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that the power of the sanctioning government to specify a court under section 197(2) is permissive and does not exclude the power of another authority to appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14. The two powers are distinct, with one concerning the "Court" and the other concerning the "person" presiding, and they are not mutually exclusive.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Special Magistrate, who was temporarily appointed as an acting Sessions Judge and then reverted to his original post, ceases to have jurisdiction over a case without a fresh notification appointing him and transferring the case.

facts: A Special Magistrate was appointed to try the petitioner's case.
This magistrate was later temporarily appointed as an acting Sessions Judge, during which time he did not handle the case.
He then reverted to his original post as Special Magistrate.
The petitioner argued that the magistrate no longer had jurisdiction over the case without a fresh government notification re-appointing him and transferring the case back to him.
application: The counsel for the State, while not agreeing with the petitioner's legal argument, informed the court that they were prepared to advise the government to issue a new notification and formally transfer the case as requested.
This action would resolve the petitioner's objection in a practical sense, regardless of its legal merit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found it unnecessary to rule on the legal merits of the objection. Because the State offered to issue a new notification, which would resolve the issue, the Court declined to pronounce a judgment on whether the magistrate had legally lost jurisdiction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the receipt of money by the appellants from the complainant at the time of an oral executory agreement of lease was a punishable offence under section 18(1) of the Act.

facts: The appellants received money from a complainant.
This transaction occurred at the time of an oral executory agreement for a lease.
law: The relevant law in question was section 18(1) of the Act.
application: The Court analyzed whether the act of receiving money under these specific circumstances (an oral, not-yet-executed lease agreement) constituted an offense under section 18(1).

The Court determined that this particular act was not made punishable by the statute and was 'outside its mischief,' meaning it did not fall within the scope of actions the law was intended to prohibit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the receipt of money by the appellants was not a punishable offense under section 18(1) of the Act. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal, overturned the convictions by the Presidency Magistrate and the High Court, and acquitted the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power of the sanctioning Government to specify a court for trial under section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code excludes the power of another authority to appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14 of the Code.
appellant_arguments: The power of the Government to specify a 'court' for trial under section 197(2) is the same as appointing a 'person' to preside, and therefore it excludes the power of another authority to appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14.
respondent_arguments: The power to specify a court under section 197(2) is a permissive power and does not exclude other powers if unexercised. Furthermore, specifying a 'court' is distinct from appointing a 'person' (Magistrate) to function in that court, so the two powers are not in conflict.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Special Magistrate, who was temporarily appointed as an acting Sessions Judge and then reverted to his original post, ceases to have jurisdiction over a case without a fresh notification appointing him and transferring the case.
appellant_arguments: The Special Magistrate, Shri K. L. Pandey, ceased to have jurisdiction over the case after he was appointed as an acting Sessions Judge. Upon reverting to his original post, a fresh notification was required to re-appoint him as the Special Magistrate for the case and to formally transfer the case back to him.
respondent_arguments: Without conceding the legal point, the State offered to advise the Government to issue the necessary notification and have the case transferred to resolve the objection.

appellant_arguments: The receipt of money at the time of an oral executory agreement of lease was not a punishable offense under section 18(1) of the Act and fell outside its scope.
respondent_arguments: The receipt of money under such circumstances was a punishable offense under section 18(1) of the Act (as implied by the convictions in the lower courts).

cases.principle: A law is discriminatory if it allows for the allotment of an individual case to a special court that is authorized to conduct the trial by a procedure substantially different from the normal procedure, thereby prejudicing the accused. The Court distinguished the present case from this principle.

cases.case_name: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
cases.principle: A lacuna (or defect) in a sanction for prosecution can be remedied during the course of the trial by the introduction of specific evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The receipt of money at the time of an oral executory agreement of lease is not a punishable act under section 18(1) of the Act and is outside its mischief.
obiter: When interpreting a document, the intention of the parties is the determining factor and must be gathered from the document itself. If the words are clear, they must be given effect, and extraneous enquiry is ruled out; however, if the language is ambiguous, it is permissible to look to surrounding circumstances.
The power of the government under section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code to specify a court for trial is a permissive power, and no implication arises from the non-exercise of that power.

A law vesting discretion in an authority to allot an individual case to a special court is not discriminatory under Article 14 of the Constitution if the trial is conducted entirely under the normal procedure.

The power under section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code is vested in the government to be exercised on grounds of convenience, complexity, or gravity of the case, not for the protection of the public servant involved.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The receipt of money by the appellants from the complainant at the time of an oral executory agreement of lease was not a punishable offense under section 18(1) of the Act. The act of receiving the money falls outside the mischief of that section, and therefore the convictions by the Presidency Magistrate and the High Court were in error.
legal_tests_applied: The test for discrimination under Article 14, as established in Anwar Ali Sarkar's case, is whether an individual case is allotted to a special court that uses a procedure substantially different from the normal procedure, thereby causing prejudice.

The test for statutory conflict between section 197(2) and section 14 of the Criminal Procedure Code is to examine their respective scopes, distinguishing between the power to specify a "Court" and the power to appoint a "person" (Magistrate).
why_appellant_lost: The challenge under Article 14 failed because the Special Magistrate under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure Code has to try the case entirely under the normal procedure, so no discrimination of the kind contemplated by the decision in Anwar Ali Sarkar's case arises.

The challenge to the validity of the sanction for prosecution was rejected as premature, because any lacuna in the sanction order could be remedied during the trial by the introduction of specific evidence.

The argument that section 197(2) CrPC excludes the power under section 14 CrPC was rejected because the two sections have different scopes: section 197(2) relates to specifying a "Court," while section 14 relates to appointing a "person." Furthermore, the power under section 197(2) is permissive, and its non-exercise does not prevent another authority from acting under section 14.

The objection to the Special Magistrate's jurisdiction was not decided upon because the State offered to issue the necessary notification to cure any potential defect, rendering a judicial pronouncement on the matter unnecessary.
why_respondent_won: The appointment of a Special Magistrate under section 14 was upheld against an Article 14 challenge because the Magistrate was bound to follow the normal trial procedure, thus creating no prejudicial discrimination.
The prosecution was allowed to proceed despite an allegedly defective sanction because the defect was deemed curable by evidence that could be presented at trial.

The State's power to appoint a Special Magistrate under section 14 was found not to be in conflict with the sanctioning Government's power under section 197(2), as the former concerns the appointment of a person and the latter concerns the specification of a court, and the power under 197(2) is discretionary, not exclusive.
The State successfully avoided a ruling on the Magistrate's jurisdiction by agreeing to issue a new notification to resolve the appellant's objection.
policy_considerations: The court determined that the policy behind section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code is not the protection of the public servant, unlike section 197(1). Instead, the power to specify a court is vested in the government for reasons of convenience, or due to the complexity or gravity of the case.

The court expressed disapproval of the practice of directly approaching the Supreme Court in matters that have already been decided by a High Court, without first obtaining leave to appeal from that decision, except for good reasons.
